prompt: The labor force is defined as the sum of which two groups?

options.label: A
options.text: Workers currently employed and workers who have given up searching for jobs

options.label: B
options.text: Adults who have worked at any point during the past 12 months

options.label: C
options.text: Full-time workers and part-time workers

options.label: D
options.text: All adults aged 16 and older, regardless of employment status

options.label: E
options.text: Employed workers and unemployed workers who are actively seeking employment

explanation: The labor force = Employed + Unemployed (actively seeking work); groups NOT in the labor force include retirees, full-time students not seeking work, stay-at-home parents, and discouraged workers - all adults who are neither employed nor actively searching.

prompt: The unemployment rate is officially defined as

options.label: A
options.text: Adults who lost jobs last month, as a percentage

options.label: B
options.text: Active job seekers as a percentage of total population

options.label: C
options.text: Unemployed people as a percentage of the labor force

options.label: D
options.text: Adults without paid jobs as a percentage of adults

options.label: E
options.text: Unemployed workers as a percentage of adult population

explanation: Unemployment rate = (Unemployed ÷ Labor Force) × 100; the denominator is the labor force (employed + unemployed), NOT the total adult population; to be counted as unemployed, a person must be jobless, available to work, and actively searching.

prompt: The labor force participation rate (LFPR) is best defined as

options.label: A
options.text: The labor force as a percentage of the adult population

options.label: B
options.text: The percentage of the adult population that is employed full time

options.label: C
options.text: The number of discouraged workers divided by the adult population

options.label: D
options.text: The percentage of the labor force that is currently employed

options.label: E
options.text: The ratio of unemployed workers to all adults in the economy

explanation: LFPR = (Labor Force ÷ Adult Population) × 100. It measures what share of the working-age population is participating in the labor market - either holding a job or actively looking for one; it does NOT distinguish between employed and unemployed within that group.

prompt: Which of the following individuals is correctly classified as UNEMPLOYED for official measurement purposes?

options.label: A
options.text: A parent who quit work three years ago to raise children and has not applied for any jobs since

options.label: B
options.text: A worker employed 10 hours per week who is not looking for more hours

options.label: C
options.text: A laid-off worker actively applying for jobs and available immediately

options.label: D
options.text: A full-time college student who is not looking for a job

options.label: E
options.text: A retired teacher who receives a pension and is not seeking work

explanation: To be officially unemployed, a person must meet all three criteria: (1) not currently employed, (2) available to work, and (3) actively searching for work. The 28-year-old satisfies all three conditions; retirees, students not searching, and those who stopped looking are classified as "not in the labor force.".

prompt: Which of the following individuals would be classified as NOT IN THE LABOR FORCE?

options.label: A
options.text: A furloughed worker expected to be recalled to work next month

options.label: B
options.text: An available worker who stopped searching because suitable jobs seem unavailable

options.label: C
options.text: A new college graduate who is available to work and attending job fairs

options.label: D
options.text: A part-time employee actively seeking a full-time position

options.label: E
options.text: A worker recently laid off who is submitting job applications every week

explanation: A person who has stopped actively searching for work because they believe no jobs are available is called a "discouraged worker." Discouraged workers are classified as "not in the labor force" - they are neither employed nor officially unemployed. This is a key limitation of the official unemployment rate.

prompt: An economy has 160 million employed workers and 10 million unemployed workers actively seeking jobs. The adult population is 220 million. What is the unemployment rate?

explanation: Labor Force = 160M + 10M = 170M; unemployment rate = (10 ÷ 170) × 100 ≈ 5.88%. Common error: dividing by adult population (220M) gives 4.55% - wrong denominator; the denominator must be the labor force, not the adult population.

prompt: Frictional unemployment is BEST described as

options.label: A
options.text: Joblessness among workers who have completely given up looking for work

options.label: B
options.text: Unemployment caused by a recession and falling aggregate demand for labor

options.label: C
options.text: Temporary unemployment during job search or entry into the labor force

options.label: D
options.text: Unemployment resulting from automation permanently replacing workers in an industry

options.label: E
options.text: Long-term joblessness resulting from a mismatch between worker skills and employer needs

explanation: Frictional unemployment reflects the time it takes to match workers with jobs - a new graduate searching for her first position, or a worker who quit to find a better job. It is temporary, voluntary in many cases, and exists even in a healthy labor market; it is NOT caused by recessions or skills mismatches.

prompt: Structural unemployment BEST describes which situation?

options.label: A
options.text: A worker who is between jobs after voluntarily quitting to search for a better position

options.label: B
options.text: A worker whose skills no longer match available jobs

options.label: C
options.text: A seasonal farmworker who is between planting and harvest seasons

options.label: D
options.text: A worker who is unemployed because the economy entered a recession

options.label: E
options.text: A factory worker temporarily laid off during a slow quarter who expects to be rehired

explanation: Structural unemployment results from a fundamental change in the economy - technological progress, industry decline, or geographic shifts - that makes certain worker skills permanently obsolete or mismatched with available jobs. Unlike frictional unemployment, it is long-lasting and typically requires workers to retrain or relocate to find new employment.

prompt: Cyclical unemployment is BEST defined as

options.label: A
options.text: Unemployment that exists in a healthy economy due to normal job transitions

options.label: B
options.text: Job losses caused by insufficient aggregate demand during a downturn

options.label: C
options.text: Unemployment equal to the natural rate of unemployment

options.label: D
options.text: Joblessness among discouraged workers who have stopped searching

options.label: E
options.text: Permanent joblessness caused by workers' skills becoming obsolete

explanation: Cyclical unemployment rises and falls with the business cycle. During recessions, falling aggregate demand causes firms to reduce production and lay off workers - creating cyclical unemployment; it disappears when the economy returns to full employment and is the primary target of stabilization policies (monetary and fiscal policy).

prompt: The natural rate of unemployment (NRU) is equal to

options.label: A
options.text: Frictional plus structural unemployment

options.label: B
options.text: The cyclical unemployment rate when the economy is operating above potential output

options.label: C
options.text: The sum of cyclical and frictional unemployment only

options.label: D
options.text: The unemployment rate during the worst point of a recession

options.label: E
options.text: Zero, because a fully functioning economy would have everyone employed

explanation: NRU = Frictional Unemployment + Structural Unemployment. It is the unemployment rate when the economy is at full employment - cyclical unemployment equals zero; it is "natural" not because it is desirable but because it reflects unavoidable labor market frictions and structural changes, not insufficient aggregate demand.

prompt: When economists say the economy is at "full employment," they mean

options.label: A
options.text: The government has achieved its unemployment target of 2 percent

options.label: B
options.text: There is zero unemployment — every adult who wants a job has one

options.label: C
options.text: The labor force participation rate equals 100 percent

options.label: D
options.text: All workers are employed in jobs that match their skill level

options.label: E
options.text: Cyclical unemployment is zero and actual unemployment equals the natural rate

explanation: Full employment does NOT mean zero unemployment; at full employment, cyclical unemployment = 0 (no recession-driven joblessness), and the actual unemployment rate = NRU. Frictional and structural unemployment still exist - workers are still changing jobs and industries are still evolving - but no cyclical unemployment results from insufficient demand.

prompt: Cyclical unemployment is calculated as

options.label: A
options.text: The labor force participation rate minus the employment rate

options.label: B
options.text: The total unemployed divided by the adult population

options.label: C
options.text: The actual unemployment rate minus the natural rate of unemployment

options.label: D
options.text: The natural rate of unemployment minus the actual unemployment rate

options.label: E
options.text: Frictional unemployment plus structural unemployment

explanation: Cyclical unemployment = Actual unemployment rate - Natural rate of unemployment; A positive result indicates the economy is operating below full employment (recessionary gap). A negative result (actual < NRU) indicates the economy is above full employment (inflationary gap); when cyclical = 0, the economy is at full employment.

prompt: A recent college graduate is actively searching for her first job in engineering. She has the skills employers want but has not yet received an offer. She BEST represents

options.label: A
options.text: Natural unemployment, because new graduates are always outside the labor force

options.label: B
options.text: Frictional unemployment during initial job search

options.label: C
options.text: Cyclical unemployment, since new graduates enter the market during economic downturns

options.label: D
options.text: Discouraged worker status, since she has not yet found a job

options.label: E
options.text: Structural unemployment, since she lacks real-world work experience

explanation: A new graduate searching for her first job is experiencing frictional unemployment - the temporary joblessness that arises from the normal matching process between workers and employers. Her skills are appropriate for the market; she simply needs time to find the right match; this is expected even in a healthy, growing economy.

prompt: A textile worker loses his job because clothing manufacturing has moved overseas and his factory permanently closed. His weaving skills have no demand in his local economy. He BEST represents

options.label: A
options.text: Natural unemployment — some job loss is inevitable in any economy

options.label: B
options.text: Structural unemployment caused by a lasting skills mismatch

options.label: C
options.text: Voluntary unemployment — he chose to work in a declining industry

options.label: D
options.text: Cyclical unemployment — the factory closed because of a recession in consumer spending

options.label: E
options.text: Frictional unemployment — he just needs to search more actively for a weaving job

explanation: Global trade shifts that permanently close domestic manufacturing represent structural change - a fundamental, long-lasting transformation of the economy that creates a mismatch between workers' existing skills and available jobs. Unlike frictional unemployment, he cannot resolve this by simply searching longer; he needs retraining or a change of occupation.

prompt: During a recession, a retail store closes and lays off 200 workers because consumer spending has fallen sharply. These workers BEST represent

options.label: A
options.text: Voluntary unemployment, since they could have found work in other sectors

options.label: B
options.text: Frictional unemployment, since they are temporarily between jobs

options.label: C
options.text: Cyclical unemployment caused by reduced aggregate demand

options.label: D
options.text: Structural unemployment, since retail is being permanently disrupted by e-commerce

options.label: E
options.text: Natural unemployment, since some retail workers are always unemployed

explanation: Layoffs caused by reduced consumer spending during a recession represent cyclical unemployment - joblessness directly tied to the business cycle. When aggregate demand falls, firms reduce output and employment; these workers have skills the economy needs; the problem is insufficient demand; when the economy recovers, demand for their labor returns.

prompt: The PRIMARY limitation of the official unemployment rate, as identified in the AP Macroeconomics CED, is that it

options.label: A
options.text: Is based on a survey that systematically undercounts employed workers

options.label: B
options.text: Excludes discouraged workers and does not capture involuntary part-time underemployment

options.label: C
options.text: Is calculated monthly rather than weekly, making it outdated

options.label: D
options.text: Overstates unemployment by including workers who are between frictionally unemployed positions

options.label: E
options.text: Overstates unemployment by including part-time workers who want fewer hours

explanation: The official unemployment rate understates true joblessness because it excludes discouraged workers (who gave up searching and are classified as "not in labor force") and counts involuntary part-time workers as "employed." Both groups represent genuine labor market hardship invisible in the headline rate.

prompt: A discouraged worker is BEST defined as a person who

options.label: A
options.text: Has been unemployed for more than 26 weeks and no longer qualifies for unemployment benefits

options.label: B
options.text: Is employed in a job below their qualifications and seeking a better position

options.label: C
options.text: Is cyclically unemployed due to a recession and waiting for economic recovery

options.label: D
options.text: Works part time but prefers full-time employment

options.label: E
options.text: Is available but has stopped searching because jobs seem unavailable

explanation: Discouraged workers are not counted in the official unemployment rate because they have stopped actively searching for work. They are classified as "not in the labor force." Because they are neither employed nor searching, their exclusion makes the official unemployment rate lower than the true extent of labor market hardship - the primary limitation of the measure.

prompt: A worker who wants a full-time job but can only find 20 hours of part-time work per week is classified in official statistics as

options.label: A
options.text: Unemployed, since they lack the full-time work they desire

options.label: B
options.text: Cyclically unemployed, since part-time work reflects weak economic conditions

options.label: C
options.text: Not in the labor force, since they work fewer than 35 hours per week

options.label: D
options.text: Structurally unemployed, since full-time positions are structurally unavailable

options.label: E
options.text: Employed, although involuntary part-time work represents underemployment

explanation: Official statistics (BLS) count any person who works at least one hour per week for pay as "employed." Involuntary part-time workers - those who want full-time jobs but can only find part-time work - are counted as employed, not unemployed. This causes the official rate to understate true labor market slack.

prompt: Which of the following individuals IS included in the labor force?

options.label: A
options.text: A full-time undergraduate student with no job and not searching for one

options.label: B
options.text: A 15-year-old who babysits on weekends for neighbors

options.label: C
options.text: A 72-year-old retired professor who does not work and is not seeking employment

options.label: D
options.text: A 31-year-old accountant working 40 hours per week

options.label: E
options.text: A stay-at-home parent who has not sought paid work in five years

explanation: The 31-year-old accountant with a full-time job is employed and thus part of the labor force. The retired professor, full-time student not searching, and stay-at-home parent are all "not in the labor force." The 15-year-old is below the age threshold (16+) used to define the adult population for labor force statistics.

prompt: An economy has Adult Population = 300 million, Employed = 185 million, and Unemployed (actively seeking) = 15 million. Calculate the unemployment rate and LFPR.

options.label: A
options.text: Unemployment rate = 8.1%; LFPR = 66.7%

options.label: B
options.text: Unemployment rate = 5%; LFPR = 61.7%

options.label: C
options.text: Unemployment rate = 5%; LFPR = 66.7%

options.label: D
options.text: Unemployment rate = 7.5%; LFPR = 66.7%

options.label: E
options.text: Unemployment rate = 7.5%; LFPR = 63.3%

explanation: Labor Force = 185M + 15M = 200M; unemployment rate = (15 ÷ 200) × 100 = 7.5%. LFPR = (200 ÷ 300) × 100 = 66.7%; common errors: using 300M as denominator for unemployment rate (gives 5%) or forgetting to include unemployed in LF for LFPR.

prompt: Which type of unemployment is the PRIMARY target of expansionary monetary and fiscal policy during a recession?

options.label: A
options.text: Natural unemployment, because it is the baseline level that all economies must achieve

options.label: B
options.text: Structural unemployment, because skill mismatches reduce productivity

options.label: C
options.text: Frictional unemployment, because it is the most prevalent type

options.label: D
options.text: Cyclical unemployment, which responds to increased aggregate demand

options.label: E
options.text: Discouraged worker unemployment, because these workers need income support

explanation: Cyclical unemployment is caused by insufficient aggregate demand - firms lay off workers because sales fall. Expansionary policy (lower interest rates, higher government spending, tax cuts) boosts demand, encourages hiring, and reduces cyclical unemployment; frictional and structural unemployment are not caused by insufficient demand and do not respond to aggregate demand stimulus.

prompt: If the actual unemployment rate equals the natural rate of unemployment, which of the following must be true?

options.label: A
options.text: The labor force participation rate equals the employment-population ratio

options.label: B
options.text: Every worker in the labor force is employed

options.label: C
options.text: Zero cyclical unemployment; the economy is at full employment

options.label: D
options.text: The unemployment rate is zero

options.label: E
options.text: Structural unemployment is greater than frictional unemployment

explanation: When actual unemployment rate = NRU, cyclical unemployment = actual - NRU = 0. This is the definition of full employment: no recession-driven unemployment; frictional and structural unemployment still exist (they sum to the NRU), but no workers are unemployed solely due to weak aggregate demand.

prompt: The actual unemployment rate is 8.5% and the natural rate of unemployment is 5.5%. What is the level of cyclical unemployment?

options.label: A
options.text: 3 percent

options.label: B
options.text: 14 percent

options.label: C
options.text: 2 percent

options.label: D
options.text: 5.5 percent

options.label: E
options.text: 8.5 percent

explanation: Cyclical unemployment = Actual rate - NRU = 8.5% - 5.5% = 3%; A positive cyclical unemployment rate indicates the economy is below full employment - there is a recessionary gap, and actual output is less than potential GDP.

prompt: The natural rate of unemployment can change over time due to

options.label: A
options.text: Changes in the overall price level and inflation expectations

options.label: B
options.text: Changes in the level of cyclical unemployment during recessions

options.label: C
options.text: Changes in demographics, search efficiency, or structural skills mismatches

options.label: D
options.text: Changes in the money supply controlled by the central bank

options.label: E
options.text: Changes in fiscal policy such as government spending and tax rates

explanation: The NRU can gradually shift due to changes in labor force characteristics. An aging workforce with less job-hopping lowers frictional unemployment (and NRU); better job-search platforms reduce search time (lower NRU); rapid technological change increases structural unemployment (raises NRU); the NRU is not permanently fixed.

prompt: Which of the following BEST illustrates frictional unemployment?

options.label: A
options.text: A hotel desk clerk laid off because tourism collapsed during a recession

options.label: B
options.text: A worker who gave up job searching after 12 months of unsuccessful efforts

options.label: C
options.text: A steel mill worker laid off because a robot performs her job more cheaply

options.label: D
options.text: A coal miner whose mine closed permanently after natural gas prices fell

options.label: E
options.text: A developer who resigned and is actively interviewing elsewhere

explanation: The software developer who voluntarily quit to find a better job is experiencing frictional unemployment - the temporary, normal joblessness associated with workers transitioning between positions. She has marketable skills and will find a new job through the normal search process; this is distinct from structural (skills mismatch) and cyclical (recession-driven) unemployment.

prompt: When the economy produces at its potential (full-employment) GDP, what is the level of cyclical unemployment?

options.label: A
options.text: Cyclical unemployment equals the natural rate of unemployment

options.label: B
options.text: Cyclical unemployment equals total unemployment minus frictional unemployment

options.label: C
options.text: Cyclical unemployment is maximized

options.label: D
options.text: Zero cyclical unemployment at potential output

options.label: E
options.text: Cyclical unemployment equals the labor force participation rate minus one

explanation: Potential GDP (full-employment output) is the level of production when cyclical unemployment = 0. The economy is using its resources efficiently within the constraints of normal labor market frictions (frictional + structural unemployment); when actual GDP = potential GDP, actual unemployment = NRU and cyclical = 0.

prompt: The formula for the unemployment rate uses which denominator?

options.label: A
options.text: The total adult population

options.label: B
options.text: The labor force — the sum of employed and unemployed workers

options.label: C
options.text: The number of employed workers only

options.label: D
options.text: The number of discouraged workers plus the unemployed

options.label: E
options.text: The total population, including children

explanation: Unemployment rate = (Unemployed ÷ Labor Force) × 100, where Labor Force = Employed + Unemployed. Using the adult population as the denominator is a very common error that produces an artificially low rate; the labor force excludes retirees, students not seeking work, discouraged workers, and other non-participants.

prompt: An automated assembly system permanently replaces 500 factory workers whose specific skills are now obsolete. These workers are experiencing

options.label: A
options.text: Frictional unemployment — they just need time to find new manufacturing jobs

options.label: B
options.text: Structural unemployment caused by technological displacement

options.label: C
options.text: Cyclical unemployment — automation causes economic downturns

options.label: D
options.text: Voluntary unemployment — they could have sought retraining before losing their jobs

options.label: E
options.text: Natural unemployment — technological displacement is always built into the NRU

explanation: Technological displacement is a leading cause of structural unemployment. The automated system permanently replaces tasks these workers performed, and their skills cannot simply be applied elsewhere without significant retraining; this is structural because the problem is a skills mismatch caused by a fundamental economic shift, not a recession or temporary job transition.

prompt: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between frictional, structural, and cyclical unemployment?

options.label: A
options.text: All three types are caused by insufficient aggregate demand

options.label: B
options.text: Frictional and structural unemployment together equal cyclical unemployment

options.label: C
options.text: Frictional and structural form the natural rate; cyclical reflects demand conditions

options.label: D
options.text: Cyclical unemployment is the only type that exists during a recession; frictional and structural disappear

options.label: E
options.text: All three types can be eliminated through expansionary monetary and fiscal policy

explanation: NRU = frictional + structural - both types exist at full employment; cyclical unemployment exists only during downturns (when actual unemployment > NRU). Crucially, frictional and structural do NOT disappear during recessions - total unemployment rises above NRU because cyclical is added; and they do NOT respond to aggregate demand stimulus.

prompt: An economy's natural rate of unemployment is 4.5%. If frictional unemployment accounts for 3 percentage points, what is structural unemployment?

options.label: A
options.text: 4.5 percent

options.label: B
options.text: 3 percent

options.label: C
options.text: 7.5 percent

options.label: D
options.text: 1.5 percent

options.label: E
options.text: 0 percent

explanation: NRU = Frictional + Structural → Structural = NRU - Frictional = 4.5% - 3% = 1.5%; this is a direct application of MEA-1.E.2. The NRU is always the sum of its two components, so knowing any two of the three values allows you to find the third.

prompt: Which of the following correctly explains why the official unemployment rate is sometimes called a "floor" on true labor market hardship?

options.label: A
options.text: Discouragement and involuntary part-time work indicate hardship beyond the official rate

options.label: B
options.text: Because the unemployment rate only counts workers who applied for unemployment insurance benefits

options.label: C
options.text: Because frictional unemployment sets a minimum level that cannot be reduced below zero

options.label: D
options.text: Because the unemployment rate cannot mathematically exceed 100 percent

options.label: E
options.text: Because the natural rate sets a floor below which actual unemployment cannot fall

explanation: The official unemployment rate (U-3) undercounts true labor market hardship by excluding: (1) discouraged workers who stopped searching, and (2) involuntary part-timers classified as "employed." Including both groups in broader measures (like U-6) always yields a higher rate. Thus, U-3 represents a floor - the true extent of distress is at least that large, and typically larger.

prompt: An economy has the following data: Adult population = 400 million; Employed (full and part-time) = 248 million; Actively unemployed = 16 million; Discouraged workers = 10 million. Calculate the official labor force, unemployment rate, and LFPR.

options.label: A
options.text: LF = 264M; Unemployment rate = 6.06%; LFPR = 66%

options.label: B
options.text: LF = 264M; Unemployment rate = 4%; LFPR = 66%

options.label: C
options.text: LF = 258M; Unemployment rate = 6.2%; LFPR = 64.5%

options.label: D
options.text: LF = 274M; Unemployment rate = 5.84%; LFPR = 68.5%

options.label: E
options.text: LF = 274M; Unemployment rate = 6.57%; LFPR = 68.5%

explanation: Discouraged workers are NOT counted in the official labor force; LF = 248M + 16M = 264M. Unemployment rate = (16 ÷ 264) × 100 ≈ 6.06%; LFPR = (264 ÷ 400) × 100 = 66%; the 10M discouraged workers are in the adult population (400M) but not in the labor force (264M).

prompt: Economy data: NRU = 5%; frictional = 3%; actual unemployment rate = 8%. Calculate structural and cyclical unemployment, and describe the state of the economy.

options.label: A
options.text: Structural = 2%; Cyclical = 5%; inflationary gap

options.label: B
options.text: Structural = 3%; Cyclical = 5%; recessionary gap

options.label: C
options.text: Structural=2%; cyclical=3%; a recessionary gap

options.label: D
options.text: Structural = 2%; Cyclical = 0%; at full employment

options.label: E
options.text: Structural = 5%; Cyclical = 8%; full employment

explanation: Structural = NRU - Frictional = 5% - 3% = 2%; cyclical = Actual - NRU = 8% - 5% = 3%. The positive cyclical unemployment (3%) indicates the economy is below full employment - a recessionary gap; actual output falls short of potential GDP.

prompt: An economy has 200 million employed, 14 million unemployed (active searchers), and an adult population of 310 million. In the next quarter, due to worsening economic conditions, 4 million currently employed workers are laid off and 2 million unemployed workers become discouraged and stop searching. What is the new unemployment rate and LFPR?

options.label: A
options.text: New rate = 7.55%; LFPR = 68.4%

options.label: B
options.text: New rate = 10%; LFPR = 65.8%

options.label: C
options.text: New rate = 10.71%; LFPR = 68.1%

options.label: D
options.text: New rate = 8%; LFPR = 70.3%

options.label: E
options.text: New rate = 9.23%; LFPR = 67.1%

explanation: After the changes, employment is 196 million, unemployment is 16 million, and the labor force is 212 million. The unemployment rate is 16/212 = 7.55 percent, and the labor force participation rate is 212/310 = 68.4 percent.

prompt: The economy is at its natural rate of unemployment of 5%. Then a severe recession begins, and the actual unemployment rate rises to 9%. Meanwhile, the NRU itself rises by 0.5 percentage points due to long-term structural changes. Calculate the new cyclical unemployment and the new NRU.

options.label: A
options.text: Cyclical = 4.5%; NRU = 5.5%

options.label: B
options.text: Cyclical = 4%; NRU = 5.5%

options.label: C
options.text: Cyclical = 4%; NRU = 5%

options.label: D
options.text: Cyclical = 3.5%; NRU = 5%

options.label: E
options.text: Cyclical = 3.5%; NRU = 5.5%

explanation: New NRU = 5% + 0.5% = 5.5% (structural changes raised it); cyclical = Actual - New NRU = 9% - 5.5% = 3.5%. The structural change increased the NRU, which reduces the measured cyclical component even though total unemployment rose; this illustrates why correctly decomposing unemployment requires the current NRU estimate.

prompt: During an economic expansion, 5 million discouraged workers decide to re-enter the labor force and begin actively searching for jobs, but none of them have found work yet. What happens to the measured unemployment rate and the LFPR in the short run?

options.label: A
options.text: Unemployment rate falls; LFPR rises

options.label: B
options.text: Unemployment rate is unchanged; LFPR rises

options.label: C
options.text: Both the unemployment rate and LFPR fall

options.label: D
options.text: Unemployment rate rises; LFPR falls

options.label: E
options.text: Both rise as returning job seekers join the labor force

explanation: When discouraged workers re-enter and begin searching (but haven't found jobs yet): (1) Labor force grows (they rejoin it) → LFPR rises. (2) Unemployed count grows (they are now actively seeking) → unemployment rate rises; paradoxically, improving confidence about job prospects temporarily raises the measured unemployment rate before these workers find employment.
